does: Scrapes the scales off the skin of a whole fish, so that none are left to catch in the mouth or to make the skin gritty.

intro.what: Scaling scrapes the overlapping scales from fish skin before further preparation.
intro.why: It teaches you to work against the direction of the scales while preserving the skin.

how: Hold the fish firmly by the tail on a board that cannot slip. A deep sink or a large tray catches the flying scales.
With the back of a knife, scrape from the tail towards the head in short firm strokes, against the way the scales lie.
Turn the fish over and do the other side. Go carefully round the fins, the belly and the base of the head, where scales hide.
Rinse the fish under cold water and run a finger from tail to head to find any scale that is left.

cues.text: The skin is smooth under a finger run from tail to head, with no rough edge.
A dry rasping sound as the scales lift. It goes quiet once the skin is bare.

mistakes.mistake: Scraping from the head towards the tail, which only presses the scales flat.
mistakes.fix: Scrape from the tail towards the head, against the scales.

mistakes.mistake: Using the sharp edge of the knife, which cuts the skin.
mistakes.fix: Use the back of the blade, in short firm strokes.

quiz.question: Why remove scales from fish skin?
choices: To avoid rough gritty scales in the finished skin.
To cut the flesh into portions.
To remove the skin along with the scales.
quiz.because: Scaling cleans the skin surface while leaving the skin itself intact.

quiz.question: Which tool movement lifts scales?
choices: Long strokes with the sharp edge from head toward tail.
Short strokes with the back of the blade from tail toward head.
Smooth strokes along the direction the scales lie.
quiz.because: Working against their overlap lifts scales; the blunt back limits cutting into the skin.

quiz.question: How can remaining scales be found after rinsing?
choices: Feel only from head toward tail.
Look only at the centre of the side.
Run a finger from tail toward head for rough edges.
quiz.because: Feeling against the scale direction catches edges that might otherwise lie flat.

quiz.question: Scraping presses scales flat instead of lifting them. What should change?
choices: Continue from head toward tail with more force.
Switch to cutting through the skin.
quiz.because: Changing direction works against the overlap and lifts the scales rather than smoothing them down.
